name: Mississippian culture
title: The story of the Mississippian culture

text: About 1,200 years ago, Native American peoples along the Mississippi River began a way of life now called the Mississippian culture.
src: a way of life that took shape in the central Mississippi valley between about 800 and 1050 CE / The Mississippian culture was a way of life shared from about 800 to 1600 by many Native American peoples

text: They grew maize, or corn, with squash and sunflowers in the rich soil of river valleys.
Women probably did most of the farming, while men hunted deer and turkey.
src: The economy rested on maize, grown with squash, sunflower and native seed plants in the fertile soils of river floodplains
women did most of the farming and men hunted and fought, and archaeologists think the division was old / Hunting deer and turkey

text: At Cahokia they built Monks Mound, about 30 metres high, carrying all the earth in baskets.
Cahokia was the largest town north of Mexico, with perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people.
src: Monks Mound at Cahokia, about 30 metres high / all the earth was carried in baskets
for more than a century it was the largest town north of Mexico / Cahokia may have held 10,000 to 20,000 people at its height

text: Chiefs lived on top of flat-topped mounds, beside open squares where people met and played a game called chunkey.
Moundville, in Alabama, had 29 mounds around a square.
src: Chiefs lived on the summits of mounds / stood around plazas used for ceremonies, councils and the game of chunkey
Moundville, on the Black Warrior River in Alabama, became a regional capital from about 1150, with 29 platform mounds around a rectangular plaza

text: Copper plates found at Etowah show the Birdman, a dancer with falcon wings.
Their art suggests they saw the world in three levels: the sky above, the world of people, and a world below.
src: The best-known figure is the Birdman, a dancer or warrior with falcon wings and a beaked mask / the winged falcon dancers on the plates from Etowah
Together the images suggest a cosmos of three levels / an Upper World of the sun, thunder beings and birds, the Middle World of people, and a Beneath World

text: Spanish soldiers attacked their towns, and later diseases and slave raids broke up the chiefdoms.
Survivors formed new nations, such as the Muscogee, and many of their great mounds still stand today.
src: De Soto’s army burns the town of Mabila after an ambush; thousands of its people die / the smallpox epidemic that began in 1696 and the slave raids encouraged by English traders / The chiefdoms that de Soto met did not survive the next century and a half.
Survivors regrouped in new confederacies, among them the Muscogee or Creek / Moundville, Etowah, Spiro and Ocmulgee are among the centres preserved as parks and historic sites
